Sometimes there is no answer column. You have hundreds of CTD profiles and no water-mass
classification, or counts of two dozen taxa at every station and no list of the habitats
they come from. Unsupervised methods find structure in the data itself: **clustering**
sorts stations into groups, and **principal component analysis** turns many columns into
a few that can be mapped or passed to a model.

[Types of learning](../01-introduction/types-of-learning.qmd) ran k-means on temperature,
salinity and depth. This section takes clustering and PCA further on a community matrix
of 24 taxa, and shows how to check what they find. Every one of these methods returns an
answer for any table, so the checks matter as much as the methods: a shuffled copy of the
data as a baseline, bootstrap samples, and variables the method never saw.

::: {#pages}

## Findings from this section

- Two k-means clusters recovered the **hard and soft seabed** from species counts alone,
  with **15 of 800** stations in the other kind's cluster.
- The average silhouette width of those clusters was **0.179**, below the rule-of-thumb
  0.25 for "no substantial structure". Shuffled counts gave a baseline of about 0.05, and
  two clusters stood furthest above it, at **3.5 times** the baseline.
- One table and one set of distances gave agreement with the seabed from **0.005** to
  **0.89**, depending only on the linkage rule. Ward's two groups matched k-means' at an
  adjusted Rand index of 0.94.
- The first two principal components held **29.4%** of the variance, which is usual for
  species counts. Depth and hard bottom both ran about **39°** from the nearest axis,
  because the two components held almost the same share.
- Three rules for the number of components kept **16**, **3** and **2**: a share of the
  variance, a shuffled baseline, and cross-validation for predicting depth. The third
  component held real structure, rock against gravel, that depth did not need.
- In **52 of 60** bootstrap samples the seabed split came back, and in 8 a depth split took
  its place. The average adjusted Rand index, 0.87, described neither.
- Splitting the soft-bottom stations came back in every bootstrap sample, yet **11%** of
  them sat near the boundary between the clusters, against **2%** for the seabed split. It
  was a cut through a depth gradient, not two groups.

::: {.callout-important}
A pattern that comes back in every bootstrap sample can still be a cut through a gradient,
because k-means cuts a steady gradient in the same place every time. Look for a gap
between the groups, and compare them with a recorded category, before calling them groups.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
Two habits run through these pages. **Run the same steps on a shuffled copy of the data**,
each column shuffled on its own, so every column keeps its values and the groups are gone:
silhouette widths and shares of the variance have no fixed scale, and the shuffled copy
gives them one. And **compare the result with a variable the method never saw**, such as
the recorded seabed. A gradient that turns up this way is a finding too: "composition
changes steadily with depth" is worth reporting.
:::


## Further resources

**Documentation**

- [tidyclust](https://tidyclust.tidymodels.org/), tidymodels. Clustering in the same specification and workflow idiom as the rest of the course.
- [Clustering](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/clustering.html), scikit-learn user guide. The comparison figure near the top, showing ten methods on the same six datasets, is worth more than the text.
- [Decomposing signals in components](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/decomposition.html), scikit-learn user guide. PCA and its relatives.
